exposure: Hours/day on electronic devices; social media use; nonscreen activities (in-person interaction, sports, homework, print, religious services)
outcome: Depressive-symptom item mean > 3; at least one suicide-related outcome (YRBS)
design: Cross-sectional correlations and relative risks; year-level co-movement
estimate: High depressive symptoms 16.13% (2010) to 21.48% (2015), +33%; 5+ h/day devices: 48% had a suicide-related outcome vs 29% at 1 h (66% more likely); 3+ h vs <=2 h: +34%; homework time negatively correlated with depressive symptoms (Table 2)
note: Correlational; homework treated as a protective nonscreen activity, not as pressure

exposure: Screen activities (social media, internet, texting, gaming) vs nonscreen (in-person interaction, sports, homework, religious services)
outcome: Psychological well-being: self-esteem, life satisfaction, happiness
design: Cross-sectional dose-response; year-level co-movement with lagged activities
estimate: Well-being fell suddenly after 2012; lower among heavier screen users and higher among nonscreen users; light electronic-communication users happiest (abstract). Press release: happiest at <1 h/day, unhappiness rises steadily beyond
verified_from: PubMed abstract (effect sizes in paper not accessible)
note: Full text not accessible from this host; dose-response numbers unverified

exposure: Digital media hours/day (<1 h light vs 5+ h heavy)
outcome: Unhappiness, low well-being, depression, suicidal ideation, attempts
design: Cross-sectional risk ratios, common analysis across datasets
estimate: Heavy vs light users 48% to 171% more likely to be unhappy/low well-being/have suicide risk factors; twice as likely to report a suicide attempt; light (not non-) users highest in well-being; largest drop between moderate and heavy use

outcome: 4-item depressive affect scale (life meaningless, future hopeless, enjoy life, good to be alive)
estimate: Girls: decline 1991-2011 then rise, peak 2018; period effect 2018 = 1.15 (p<.01); increase 2012-2018 about 0.50 SD for girls (mean 7.26 to 8.39) and 0.33 SD for boys; cohort effects minimal
note: No exposure variables; establishes the trend and its period (not cohort) nature

study: Kreski, Platt, Rutherford, Olfson, Odgers, Schulenberg & Keyes
exposure: Daily social media use (visit social networking sites almost every day) vs less
estimate: Girls overall OR 1.03 (0.97-1.09) for score>9, 1.01 (0.95-1.08) for >10, 1.02 for >12, 1.07 (0.96-1.21) for >15; boys OR 0.97 (0.92-1.02) ... 0.86 (0.76-0.98) for >15; possible harm confined to 2009-2010; daily use rose 61% to 89% (girls) and 46% to 75% (boys)
note: Exposure is frequency, not hours; cannot test an hours dose or a homework interaction

study: Kreski, Chen, Olfson, Cerda, Martins, Mauro, Branas, Rajan & Keyes
exposure: Six latent time-use groups from 17 items (dates, parties, evenings out, friends, social media, sports, homework, work ...)
design: Latent profile analysis; survey-weighted logistic regression by decade; counterfactual decomposition
estimate: Internalizing symptoms higher with low socializing, low engagement (sports, academics, community service) and paid work; social engagement declined over time, but shifts in time-use groups did not account for much of the increase in depressive symptoms (abstract)
note: Homework hours are one of 17 profile items, not a separate exposure

outcome: Internalizing factor (8 items incl. self-derogation) and externalizing factor
design: Factor analysis; time-varying regression by sex
estimate: Internalizing factor mean -0.03 (2012) to 0.06 (2013); externalizing -0.06 (2011) to -0.13 (2012); internalizing-externalizing coupling fell 22.3% 2010-2018; decoupling started ~1995 for boys, ~2010 for girls
note: Documents the 2012 break for girls specifically

study: Kaur, Hamilton, Chen, Hasin, Cerda, Martins & Keyes
exposure: Yearly prevalence of getting 7+ hours of sleep most nights
outcome: Loneliness (A lot of times I feel lonely); self-esteem, self-derogation, depressive affect
estimate: Loneliness +0.83% per year; 2019 log-odds 0.68 (0.49-0.87) above the period mean; girls steeper than boys (p<.0001); period-effect median OR 1.16 before vs 1.07 after adjusting for 7+ h sleep
note: Sleep explains part of the period rise in loneliness; sleep itself fell most in the 1990s (Keyes 2015)

outcome: Gets 7+ hours of sleep; gets less sleep than should
estimate: Sleep declined over 20 years; largest change between 1991-1995 and 1996-2000; girls, minorities, urban and low-SES students less likely to report 7+ h

exposure: New-media screen time (devices, social media, online news); homework, work, TV
estimate: 16-17% more likely to report short sleep in 2015 vs 2009 (35% to 41% and 37% to 43%); exposure-response after 2+ h/day of device use; homework, paid work and TV stable or falling over the period
relevance: H1 (sleep channel); against H2 via homework time
note: Homework time flat 2009-2015 by the authors' account

outcome: Self-esteem, depressed mood, GPA, homework hours, evenings out, work, sports, volunteering
estimate: Homework hours declined steadily 1991-2014 (coefficient +0.55 in 1991 vs 2008; under 5 h/week by 2014); evenings out OR 1.29 (1991) to 0.67 (2014); depressed mood +0.13 in 2014

journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 36(6):1892-1913
exposure: In-person peer interaction (friends, parties, going out, dating, movies, riding in cars); social media use
estimate: 2010s teens spent less time in in-person interaction; college-bound seniors in 2016 an hour less per day than late 1980s despite little change in homework or extracurricular time; loneliness rose sharply after 2011; lowest in-person + highest social media = most lonely; in-person interaction and social media positively correlated at the individual level
note: Homework time described as little changed for 12th graders

exposure: Adult activities (dating, sex, alcohol, paid work, going out without parents, driving)
estimate: Fewer adolescents engage in adult activities; trends unlikely due to homework and extracurricular time, which stayed steady or declined

outcome: Well-being (happiness, depressive affect, self-esteem; 12 MTF items)

note: The public R code lists the MTF 8th/10th V-codes used here (see notes/mtf.md)

exposure: Social media vs TV vs gaming, by sex
design: Matters Arising: argues six analytic choices lowered effect sizes; reports r by sex and medium
estimate: Figure 2 gives average linear r for boys and girls by medium; values behind paywall
note: Numbers not verifiable from this host

mtf_sample: UK Millennium Cohort age 14 (n = 11,427), not MTF
exposure: Hours/day on social media, internet, gaming, TV
outcome: Self-harm, depressive symptoms, life satisfaction, self-esteem
estimate: Heavy internet users 166% more likely to have clinically relevant depressive symptoms (girls) vs 75% (boys); social media/internet stronger than gaming/TV
note: Not MTF; included because it is the sex-by-activity benchmark cited with the MTF work

study: Kreski, Askari, Cerda, Chen, Hasin, Martins, Mauro, Olfson & Keyes
exposure: Six time-use profiles from 17 behaviour items
design: Latent profile analysis; sex-stratified yearly means 2010-2020
estimate: Poor self-esteem rose across nearly all activity groups; increases most pronounced for girls with low peer socializing
relevance: H1/H2: rise is not confined to any time-use group
note: Most recent MTF time-use paper found

journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 65(4):384-407
exposure: Established and novel risk factors incl. digital technology and social media
design: Annual Research Review with epidemiological criteria for causes of increases
estimate: Concludes many potential causes; digital technology evidence does not yet meet all conditions for explaining the increase (Table 2)
